client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. The sadness just kind of sits on me all the time, like this heavy weight I can't shake, and I keep finding myself questioning what the point of everything is for me going forward. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, honestly, because nothing really feels like it can change the fact that she's gone.
therapist: I'm so sorry for the loss of your grandmother — what you're carrying right now sounds deeply painful, like a grief that's settled into every part of your day, and that questioning of "what's the point" makes complete sense when someone so meaningful is gone. You're right that nothing we talk about will undo her passing, and I want to honor that truth rather than gloss over it — but sometimes putting words to this kind of weight can help us understand what we're really missing and what she meant to our sense of purpose. I'm wondering, when you think about her and the life you shared, what feels most lost to you beyond her physical presence?

client: I think what I miss most is that she was the one person who never made me feel like I had to explain myself. Like, I could just show up at her house and exist, and that was enough for her. Without her, there's this silence where that acceptance used to be, and I don't really have anyone else in my life who fills that space.
therapist: What you're describing is such a profound and specific kind of love — that rare feeling of being completely enough just as you are, without needing to perform or justify yourself — and it makes sense that losing her feels like losing something irreplaceable, not just a person but a whole way of being seen. That quiet ache you're sitting with right now, that stillness where her acceptance used to live, is worth paying attention to. I'm curious — when you think about that feeling she gave you, of just being enough, do you ever experience even small moments of that with yourself, or does that sense of acceptance feel like it only ever came from her?

client: Honestly, no, I don't really feel that with myself. I'm actually pretty hard on myself most of the time, and I think part of why her acceptance meant so much was because it felt like a counterweight to all the criticism I carry around in my own head. So now without her, it's like that critical voice just gets louder and there's nothing pushing back against it anymore.
therapist: What you've just named is really important — it sounds like your grandmother wasn't just a person you loved, but she was also serving as an external anchor against a very harsh inner critic that's been there for a long time. Now that she's gone, that critic has the floor to itself, and part of what we might gently explore together is how to start building some of that counterweight from the inside, so it doesn't have to live only in someone else. I'm wondering — what does that critical voice most often say to you, and do you have any sense of where it learned to be so loud?

client: The voice mostly tells me I'm a burden to people, that I ask for too much or take up too much space, and that people only tolerate me rather than actually wanting me around. I think it probably comes from my parents, who were pretty critical and not very emotionally available when I was growing up. But I guess what I'm skeptical about is this idea of building that counterweight from the inside, because I've tried being kinder to myself before and it just feels fake, like I'm lying to myself.
therapist: That skepticism makes a lot of sense, and I want to validate it — if you've spent a lifetime being told implicitly that you're too much, telling yourself "actually I'm wonderful" probably does feel like putting a bandage over something much deeper. What I'd gently offer is that building a counterweight doesn't have to mean forcing positive feelings that don't feel true; it can start with something smaller, like just questioning whether the critical voice is actually accurate, the way a good lawyer might cross-examine a witness. For instance, that belief that people only tolerate you rather than want you around — I'm curious, is there any evidence in your life, even small moments, that actually contradicts that story?

client: I mean, I guess my grandmother herself is evidence of that, because she genuinely seemed to want me around, not just tolerate me. And there's a coworker who texts me sometimes just to share things she finds funny, which I suppose isn't something you'd do with someone you merely tolerate. But the tricky part is my brain immediately explains those away, like my grandmother had to love me because she was family, and my coworker is just being friendly, so it doesn't really land as proof the way you'd hope it would.
therapist: You actually did something really significant just now — you found the evidence, which isn't easy, and then you watched your mind immediately move to discredit it, and you noticed that happening in real time. That noticing is actually the skill we're trying to build, because that dismissal — "she had to love me, she's just being friendly" — is the critical voice protecting itself, and it's worth asking why it works so hard to reject any information that might threaten it. What do you think it would mean for you, or what might feel scary, if you actually let that evidence count?

client: I think if I let that evidence count, it would mean I'd have to take some responsibility for how isolated I feel, because I couldn't just blame it on nobody wanting me around. That's actually kind of terrifying, because the loneliness is painful but it's also familiar, and if it turns out people do want me around and I'm still lonely, then the problem is something inside me that I don't know how to fix. It feels safer somehow to believe the world is closed off to me than to consider that I might be the one keeping the door shut.
therapist: What you just said takes real courage to look at — that the story of a closed world, as painful as it is, has been protecting you from something that feels even scarier, which is the uncertainty of change and the vulnerability of actually reaching toward people. But I want to gently reframe something: if you are the one holding the door, that's not a verdict on something broken inside you — it's actually hopeful, because doors you're holding can be opened, even slowly and carefully, in ways a world that simply rejects you never could be. What do you think it would feel like to experiment, just once, with letting someone in a little — maybe even that coworker — without explaining it away afterward?

client: I think it would feel terrifying, honestly, because the moment I reach out I'm exposed, and if she doesn't respond the way I hope, that critical voice is going to use it as evidence that I was right all along. I'm also not sure what "letting someone in" even looks like in practice, because there's a big gap between texting about funny things and actually being vulnerable with someone. I guess I'm worried I'd either do it wrong or it would confirm my worst fears, and I don't know if I'm in a strong enough place right now, with my grandmother's loss still so fresh, to handle that kind of risk.
therapist: Your caution here is really wise, not fearful — you're grieving, you're already carrying a lot, and this isn't the moment to force a leap into vulnerability that could feel destabilizing. What I'd actually suggest is something much smaller than vulnerability: not a heart-to-heart, but just responding to your coworker's next funny text with a little more of yourself than usual, maybe sharing something back, and then practicing *not* explaining it away when she responds warmly. The goal right now isn't to fix the loneliness or prove the critical voice wrong — it's just to collect tiny, honest data points while you're also giving yourself permission to grieve. What would feel like a manageable, small-enough step that wouldn't leave you too exposed?

client: Maybe I could just share something back when she texts, like mention something I actually found funny that week instead of just reacting to what she sends. That feels small enough that it's not really putting myself out there in a scary way. But I notice I'm already thinking about how I'll probably second-guess hitting send, or reread her response ten times trying to figure out if she's just being polite, so I'm not sure how I stop my brain from doing that part.
therapist: You've just identified the exact right step *and* the exact obstacle, which tells me you know yourself really well — that second-guessing and rereading isn't something you need to stop so much as something you can learn to notice without obeying. When you find yourself rereading her response for hidden meaning, that's actually a moment to gently ask yourself: "am I looking for truth here, or am I just giving the critical voice a chance to find something to work with?" What do you think it would take to set a small rule for yourself, like allowing one read of her response and then consciously choosing what you *want* to believe it means, rather than what the critic insists it must mean?

client: I like the idea of a one-read rule, but I'm honestly not sure I have enough control over my own brain to actually stop after one read, because it feels more like a compulsion than a choice. It's like knowing you shouldn't check if the stove is off for the fifth time but doing it anyway, that kind of thing. I guess I'm also a little unsure whether choosing what I want to believe is really any different from the fake positivity problem we talked about earlier, where it just feels like I'm forcing myself to see something that isn't there.
therapist: That's a really sharp distinction you're drawing, and it's worth taking seriously — there is a difference between forcing fake positivity and what I'm actually suggesting, which is closer to choosing *not to over-interrogate* something that has a perfectly reasonable innocent explanation, like a friend responding warmly to a text. The stove analogy is actually really apt, because what helps with that kind of compulsive checking isn't willpower so much as gently redirecting your attention to something else before the loop gets going — so the one-read rule might work better as "one read, then I put my phone down and do one concrete thing," rather than relying on your brain to just stop on its own. Does that feel more workable, and do you notice what it is you're really searching for when you reread — is it reassurance, or are you bracing for something?

client: I think I'm mostly bracing for something, honestly, like I'm scanning for the thing that confirms she doesn't actually care, because at least then I'd know and could stop hoping. The "one read, then do one concrete thing" feels more realistic than just telling my brain to stop, because it gives me somewhere to put my attention instead. But I'm a little worried that the concrete thing will just become another way of distracting myself from feelings I probably need to sit with at some point, especially with everything I'm carrying about my grandmother right now.
therapist: What you just said about bracing for rejection so you can "stop hoping" is so honest and so human — hope feels dangerous when you've learned that disappointment is more reliable than warmth, and in a way your brain is trying to protect you by finding the bad news first. You're also right that distraction and processing are different things, and I don't want the concrete action to become a way of burying feelings that need air — the grief about your grandmother, the loneliness, all of it deserves space too, just not necessarily in the moment you're rereading a text at midnight. What if we thought of it as two separate practices: the one-read-then-redirect for managing the checking compulsion, and also carving out some intentional time, maybe even in our sessions, to actually sit with what you're carrying rather than accidentally sitting with it in moments that aren't safe or supported?
